items.text: Baan Noi costs around $22 a head. Fair enough for what you get. Order the pad see ew. Good texture and the noodles taste like actual food. Don't bother with the green curry. It's loaded with sugar, cloying stuff. Not the only thing that dragged the meal down. Friday wait was long and the kitchen was clearly in over its head. If you go in you'll get a decent meal but have to put up with slow service. You can get the same result at a bunch of other places around town. The good stuff here is just too easy to get at the bad. I'd rather eat somewhere that gets both right.

Hi guys. So I was planning to see O, but it was on hiatus so we ended up booking La Rêve. We were at the Encore so the theatre was easy walk, and our seats were around third row. I knew La Rêve is often compared to O, or maybe even derivative of it, so figured it was a good substitute. It isn't O but it's a solid sub. La Rêve may have a story I guess but I did not get it, and it didn't bother me. There's a pre-show act, a funny lizard looking performer swims in the pool, stays very still for a while like a statue, and then sneaks up and sprays front rows. Main show is the draw really. Pool with platforms that go up and down, swimming, diving, walking on water, and a dive from like 25 feet above the pool. If you're looking for a big Vegas show but not paying Cirque prices, it's a good alternative. I left impressed.

If you're after a big Vegas show but not paying the massive Cirque du Soleil prices, I recommend La Rêve as a worthy alternative. We left impressed.

So a rain gauge works by catching rain with a circular opening of known area, funnels it into a tube marked in mm or inches. That depth reading is what it would look like if rain fell evenly with no runoff or soakage. Opening is often wider than the tube, so you have a narrower column to make light rain easier to read. Scale is adjusted for the difference in area. So the reading still represents actual depth. But a lot of times its placement is not good enough, and its not read soon enough after the storm so the water will evaporate. Near trees or fences it will collect less or more due to sheltering or splashing. So you have to be careful.

So these little gauges work by catching rain through a circular opening of known area. The water goes into a measuring tube marked in depth units, millimeters or inches. The reading is basically how deep the rain would be if it fell evenly over the ground with no runoff or soaking in. The opening is usually wider than the measuring tube, which concentrates the water into a narrower column, makes small amounts easier to read. The scale on the tube is adjusted for the difference in area, so the reading is actual rainfall depth. But there are two common causes of inaccurate readings. Poor placement and evaporation. Gauges near trees, buildings, or fences can collect too little or too much rain because of sheltering or splashing. And if the water is not read soon after the storm, some of it evaporates.

Rain gauges are simple in practice. It's a circle of known area. Rain gets caught, and then it goes through a spout and drops into a tube. And that tube has a scale in inches or millimeters. And that tells you how deep it would have been had it fallen evenly on the ground. No runoff, no soak-in. But the opening is often much bigger than the tube itself. This just concentrates all the rain into a much smaller column, making it easier to read smaller amounts. So the scale on the tube is adjusted for the difference in area. So it still tells you the actual depth of the rain. There are a couple of problems with rain gauges. One is placement. If your rain gauge is near trees or buildings or fences, it's not going to be very accurate. It might be sheltered, or it might splash. Also evaporation. If you don't read the rain gauge right after the rain, some of the rain will evaporate.

Marguerite found the book. Same place as every Thursday, wedged between the flour bins and the cooling racks, like it crawled in through the wall. Field Guide to Coastal Birds, spine cracked, faded library stamp inside. Overdue by now. Eleven Thursdays. She asked the day staff, checked the locks, once stayed late with a thermos and rolling pin. But no luck. The book appears between 2 and 4am and she never caught it. Tonight it felt heavier. She opened it and a receipt square slid out. I keep meaning to bring it back to the library but I walk past your window on the way and the light is on and I think somebody is awake. So I leave it here instead. Sorry. Will stop if you ask me to. She read it twice. Behind her ovens ticking. First trays of rye waiting under their cloths. She flipped the receipt over, found the pencil stub behind her ear. Wrote on the back. Don't stop. Tucked it inside the cover, set the book on the sill by the front window. Left the light on.

2:40 am. That sour smell of fermenting rye, it just washes out the floor bleach smell. Arthur wiped his palms on his jeans. He reached behind the wicker bannetons and there it was, the library's copy of The Count of Monte Cristo, taped up, on the bottom wire rack. Fourth Thursday. Like all the others, its spine was flush with the steel edge. He pulled it free. There was a square of blue prescription notepad stuck to the cover, ballpoint ink written through the paper. It said, the baker in chapter five reminds me of you. Thank you for keeping the lights on. Arthur's thumb traced the deep indentations of the pen strokes. Only sound was the compressor shuddering. A slip of paper drifted down from the back of the book. Yellowing due-date card, stamped in faded red ink. Three days overdue. He walked over to the prep table. Grabbed a warm cinnamon roll, glaze-mapped, wrapped it in parchment paper. Slipped it into his coat pocket next to the book.

There was a milk crate by the back door, that was the book drop. Every Thursday around 2, Imre would find something in it that wasn't milk. First week was a field guide to mushrooms of the Northeast, had a Carver Street Library stamp on the flyleaf, due date long past. Second week, same book. Third week, same book. He'd stopped reshelving it in his head. It lived on the flour bench now, between the scale and the tub of rye starter, cover gone soft with dough-dusted thumbprints.

Tonight he slid the crate out with his hip, hands still in oven mitts, and the book was there again, heavier than usual. A yellow square of paper stuck out near page 112. He peeled off the mitts. The note was in pencil, small, slanted hard to the right. It said your door smells better than the library. I keep meaning to bring it to the right place. Is the morel on this page the one you use? -T.

Imre looked at the page. Someone had circled nothing, the morel sat there, wrinkled and brown. He pulled the pencil from behind his ear, flipped the note over, and wrote No. Never used one. Then, after a moment, he added Come at five, there's bread. He pressed it back into the book.

So I paid 38 bucks for this second hand mechanical keyboard. Hope was low really. Just wanted no missing keycaps, no sticky grime, switches that didn't feel like gravel. On that scale it did fine. It showed up clean enough to put on my desk without a deep cleaning project and the keys have a pleasant weight to them. I type long emails a lot. And this board is actually comfortable for that. My fingers don't feel beat up after a long stretch, which is more than I can say for some newer cheap keyboards.

Rough edges not hidden though. Space bar rattles every time I catch it off centre, loose little clack that makes the whole board sound cheaper than it feels. One key repeats now and then. Look up and find an extra letter in the middle of a sentence. Not constant but irritating.

Communication was another weak spot. I asked the seller what switches it had, answer came a week later, after I'd already pulled a keycap and checked for myself. Thought about returning it. Then pictured packing it up and paying to ship it back. For 38 I kept it. Flawed but usable.

I've been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life, well, the under 21 version of it, so I sat through a lot of shows before I could even gamble. Lereve at the Wynn is one I finally caught and honestly? Mixed, maybe slightly worse than mixed. First the good, the circular stage is genuinely smart. You're basically looking down into it, so from essentially any seat you get a decent view. That's rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too, the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not in a rip-off way exactly, just if you've seen Cirque you've seen comparable feats done with maybe more clarity. And clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don't know. There's a dream maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you and the show never tells you what it's trying to say. Also there's way too much happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many wow moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing, more must be better, so they crammed everything in. Ticket note. If you're staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal, $99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn't pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts it was just average. I wasn't blown away and I don't think anyone else was either. That said, a few friends liked it, and if you've never seen it maybe check it out. Just don't expect to leave overwhelmed.

I got a second hand mechanical keyboard for 38 dollars. Was not expecting perfection, and that's what I got. It came reasonably clean, and it worked right out of the box which was a relief. The typing feel is actually better than I expected for the price. I do lots of emails for work, and my hands don't get tired after an hour or two of typing.

There's a couple of issues though. The space bar rattles, and it's pretty noticeable, especially when you hit it near the edges. Makes the whole board sound cheaper than it feels. Another key occasionally repeats, so I have to go back and delete the extra letter. Doesn't happen every time, but it does happen enough to mention.

The seller did answer my question about the switches, but it took a full week by which point I had basically figured it out myself. I considered returning it, but for 38 bucks, shipping it back didn't seem worth the trouble. I kept it because it's comfortable and usable, just not flawless.

It was 3:40am, second batch of rye proofing, and Marisol found the book again on the flour bin by the back door, its jacket cold from the alley. Fourth Thursday in a row now. Same book, A Field Guide to Night Birds, Eastgate branch, fresh due date slip each time. She'd put it in the return box on her way home every week, and by next Thursday somebody would check it out again and carry it back. She scraped dough off her knuckles and opened it. An index card fell out from the barn owls page, next to the bit that says call is a long harsh scream, with a penciled check. Card said: You leave the vent fan on, alley smells like bread till 5. I walk my mother's dog at 3:30 because she can't do it anymore. Heard one of these behind the dumpster. I keep checking this out again. Signed R. She read it twice while the oven timer counted down. Outside the fan was rattling steam over the wet dumpster lid. She flipped the card over and grabbed the grease pencil she uses for marking trays and wrote: Rye out at 4:15. Then she wrapped a heel from yesterday's loaf in wax paper, put it on the outside step, laid the book on top, propped the back door open an inch.

Marisol was at 3:40 a.m. The second batch of rye was proofing, and she found it again. The library book on the flour bin by the back door, its plastic jacket cold from the alley. Fourth Thursday in a row. Same book, A Field Guide to Night Birds, Eastgate Branch, and a fresh due-date slip every time. She kept dropping it in the return box on her way home each week and by the next Thursday someone checked it out again and brought it back to the bakery.

She scraped dough off her knuckles and opened it. A folded index card fell out from the barn owl page, next to where somebody had penciled a check beside call: a long, harsh scream.

It said: You leave the vent fan on. The alley smells like bread until five. I walk my mother's dog at half past three, because she can't anymore. Heard one of these behind the dumpster. I keep checking this out again. —R.

She read it twice. The oven timer counted down. Outside the fan rattled steam across the wet dumpster lid. She turned the card over and wrote with the grease pencil she uses to mark trays: Rye's out at 4:15. Then she wrapped a heel from yesterday's loaf in wax paper, put it on the outside step, laid the book on top and propped the back door open an inch.

I paid 38 dollars for this keyboard, used. Going in I knew 38 doesn't buy perfection. It didn't. The space bar rattles. Not every press but often enough that I hear it in the pause before a sentence starts. And one key repeats now and then, I type a word and find a doubled letter in the middle of it. So I reread everything before I hit send. Probably saved me from mistakes, but I'd rather the keyboard hadn't forced the habit.

I asked the seller about the switches before buying, answer came a week later, had already ordered it and was working out the feel myself. What keeps it on the desk is comfort. I write long emails, run past the point where I stop paying attention to my hands, this board doesn't tire them out. The keys have a weight I like. After an hour I'm still going at the same pace.

Thought about shipping it back. Kept it. The rattle annoys me less than packing a box.
